To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) subjective ratings of the orthographic similarity of words and brands are predicted by metrics from the visual word processing literature; (b) subjective ratings of orthographic similarity are higher when words share beginnings (e.g., CAT and CAMP) than when they share endings (e.g., BIRD and BIRTH); (c) shared pronunciation of the first vowel has small effects on ratings, and (d) a behavioral task confirms the similarity of shared beginning letters in lexical processing.
the ratings of orthographic similarity for word pairs and brand name pairs are predicted by metrics of visual orthographic similarity based on the number and position of shared letters.

(1) orthographic (spelled) similarity ratings of words and brand names were higher for pairs that shared initial letters rather than final letters, (2) ratings were higher when the shared letters were in a more prominent position (e.g., the first 3 letters of a 6-letter word), and (3) the ratings were strongly predicted by orthographic metrics of similarity from the visual-word identification literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the subjective perception of brand similarity and the objective measures of brand similarity.
the subjective perception of orthographic similarity between word or brand names.
the subjective and objective measures of brand name similarity and the role of orthographic similarity in determining brand name confusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the more letters two words or brand names have in common the more similar they are, and the more similar they will be judged.
brand names that are orthographically similar are more likely to be confused than brand names that are not.
orthographic similarity is a key factor in determining brand name confusion, and that this is a useful measure in determining whether brand names are too similar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
orthographic similarity is a powerful predictor of perceived brand name similarity and brand confusion.
the similarity of word pairs and brand name pairs is best predicted by a metric of orthographic similarity based on shared initial letters.
the more letters a pair of words or brand names share, the more similar they will be perceived.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orthographic similarity metric is a useful tool for determining the likelihood of confusion between brands.
the orthographic similarity of brand names can be reliably measured, and that this measure is strongly predicted by metrics based on the number and positions of shared letters.
orthographic similarity is a powerful predictor of brand name confusion, even when the pronunciation of the brand names are different.
